editorial_sections.h2: Where the Yin Yang Symbol Comes From
paragraphs: The yin-yang concept originates in ancient Chinese cosmology and became central to Taoist philosophy: the idea that seemingly opposing forces (dark and light, passive and active, feminine and masculine) aren't really in conflict, but complementary halves of a single whole, each containing a "seed" of the other. That seed is represented by the small dot of the opposite color nested inside each half of the symbol.

The classic circular swirl design, formally called a taijitu, reached its familiar swirling form in the Ming Dynasty (roughly the 14th to 16th century CE), building on an 11th-century Song Dynasty diagram, though the underlying philosophical concept it illustrates is far older. It remains one of the most recognized symbols from Chinese philosophy anywhere in the world today.

faq.q: What does the yin yang symbol mean?
faq.a: It represents the idea, central to Chinese philosophy and Taoism, that seemingly opposite forces (dark and light, passive and active, feminine and masculine) are actually complementary and interconnected. The small dot of each color inside the opposite half shows that each force contains a "seed" of the other.

faq.q: How old is the yin yang symbol?
faq.a: The underlying yin-yang philosophical concept traces back to ancient Chinese cosmology, but the classic circular swirl design (called a taijitu) took its modern recognizable form in the Ming Dynasty, roughly the 14th to 16th century CE, building on an earlier Song Dynasty diagram by Zhou Dunyi (11th century).

faq.q: How do you type the yin yang symbol?
faq.a: It falls outside the simple four-digit Windows Alt-code range. Use the Alt+X hex method in Word (type 262F, then press Alt+X), the Character Map, or copy it directly from a reference page. In HTML, use ☯: there's no short named entity.
